principle_name: Persist Through Five Contacts Before Expecting a Decision
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: When a prospect is currently buying from an established, incumbent supplier and shows early hesitation or resistance to switching or engaging with a new vendor.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect has already given a clear, final no, or when continuing contact would violate an explicit request to stop.
principle: Most first purchases from a new supplier happen only after roughly five separate points of contact; the majority of salespeople give up after one or two attempts, which is why persistence itself becomes a competitive advantage rather than a nuisance.
recommended_action: Plan a follow-up cadence of at least five meaningful touches before concluding the account is not winnable, and treat early resistance as expected friction rather than a final answer.
example: A vendor calling on an OEM purchase manager who already has approved suppliers should expect the real opening to appear only after multiple visits, not the first meeting.
counter_example: Abandoning outreach to a promising account after one unanswered email or one lukewarm first meeting.
motm_application: Directly supports MOTM-K12 (Follow-Up Framework) and the 'no_response'/'long_sales_cycle' problem categories — gives BD reps and Sales Engineers a concrete benchmark (5+ touches) rather than an arbitrary follow-up cadence.

principle_name: "Let Me Think It Over" Signals Loss, Not Deliberation
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: Whenever a prospect responds to a proposal or pitch with a vague deferral rather than a specific objection.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect has given a specific, named reason for delay (budget cycle, pending internal approval, a named blocker) — that is a real objection to work with, not a brush-off.
principle: When a prospect says they want to "think it over," they are rarely going to spontaneously revisit the decision — in practice they generally forget the details almost immediately after the meeting ends, so a vague deferral usually functions as a polite decline rather than genuine deliberation.
questions_to_ask: What specifically would you want to think over?
Is there a particular concern I can address right now?
recommended_action: Treat 'let me think it over' as a cue to surface the real, specific objection in the moment rather than scheduling a passive follow-up and waiting.
example: A prospect who says he needs to discuss it with his team should be asked directly what aspect needs discussion, rather than being left to 'get back to you.'
counter_example: Ending the meeting on 'sounds good, let me think it over' and simply waiting a week before following up.
motm_application: Useful for MOTM-K11 (Objection Handling) and the 'proposal_stalled' problem category — reframes a common vague deferral as a signal to probe rather than politely wait.

principle_name: Rejection Is Aimed at the Offer, Not the Person
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: When a salesperson is hesitating to make calls, follow up, or approach a difficult account because of fear of a negative reaction.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to the prospect-facing interaction itself — this is an internal mindset principle for the salesperson, not something to say to a customer.
principle: A prospect's 'no' is directed at the offer, price, or timing — not at the salesperson personally; roughly 80 percent of sales calls end in some form of no, and this is a normal statistical outcome rather than evidence of personal failure.
recommended_action: Separate rejection of the offer from self-worth; use rejection as a data point about fit or timing, not as a reason to reduce prospecting activity.
example: A rep who gets turned away by a purchase manager should log the reason and move to the next account rather than avoiding similar accounts afterward.
counter_example: Reducing call volume or avoiding a certain type of prospect after a string of rejections out of fear rather than data-driven reasoning.
motm_application: Supports coaching content around prospecting activity and account-entry resilience (MOTM-K06, K15) — most relevant as internal rep mindset guidance rather than a customer-facing tactic.

principle_name: Build Rapport Before Presenting the Offering
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: At the start of any new sales relationship, before product or service details are introduced.
when_not_to_use: When the buyer has explicitly asked to skip straight to commercial or technical specifics and rapport-building would waste their time.
principle: Buyers generally will not seriously engage with a pitch until they are convinced the salesperson is acting in their interest; leading with product or service details before establishing that trust tends to reduce receptiveness rather than build it.
questions_to_ask: What matters most to you in a supplier relationship?
What has gone wrong with vendors in the past?
recommended_action: Open new prospect conversations by understanding the buyer's situation and interests before introducing the product or service.
example: In a first meeting with an OEM's vendor development contact, spend the opening minutes on their sourcing priorities before presenting capabilities.
counter_example: Opening a cold call immediately with a capabilities pitch before understanding anything about the buyer's situation.
motm_application: Reinforces MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework) — supports a discovery-first opening sequence for both BD and Sales Engineer conversations.

principle_name: Small, Consistent Edges Compound Into Large Income Differences
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: When coaching a rep on incremental skill improvement rather than searching for one dramatic technique to fix performance.
when_not_to_use: Not a tactic for a specific customer conversation — this is a coaching/development principle for the salesperson.
principle: Top performers are typically not dramatically more talented than average performers; a small, consistent edge in each part of the sales process compounds over time into a very large gap in results, similar to a horse winning a race 'by a nose' but earning a vastly larger prize.
recommended_action: Coach reps to improve marginally across every stage of the process (discovery questions, objection responses, follow-up discipline) rather than expecting one big change to transform results.
example: A rep who slightly improves their discovery questions, follow-up cadence, and closing language simultaneously will see outsized gains versus improving only one area.
counter_example: Expecting a single new closing line or script to fix an underperforming pipeline.
motm_application: Useful framing for BD/Sales Engineer coaching and onboarding — supports incremental skill-building programs rather than one-off training pushes.

principle_name: Self-Talk Before a Call Affects How It Goes
author: Brian Tracy
when_to_use: Immediately before a difficult call or meeting, especially with a nervous or less-experienced rep.
when_not_to_use: Not a substitute for actual preparation, product knowledge, or account research — it complements rather than replaces those.
principle: A salesperson's internal state going into a call — confident and prepared versus anxious and unprepared — tends to carry through into tone, body language, and pacing during the interaction, which the buyer picks up on.
recommended_action: Have reps briefly mentally prepare and review their objective before walking into a meeting, rather than walking in cold or rushed.
example: A rep pausing for two minutes to review the account and their objective before a first meeting is more likely to come across as composed.
counter_example: Walking into a high-stakes first meeting directly from an unrelated stressful call with no reset in between.
motm_application: Minor supporting principle for MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework) — best used as a coaching note rather than a standalone card in customer-facing recommendations.
